blindSummary:
This is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a transgender person to be discovered in. Under an uncodified legal system derived from religious law, same-sex conduct is punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment, and transgender expression itself is criminalised through "imitation of the opposite sex" and public-morality provisions that police and religious morality-enforcement officers apply with broad discretion. There is no legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care is banned.

Enforcement is documented and brutal: trans women have been arrested, detained, and tortured on morality grounds; a trans elder from a foreign labour-migrant community died in custody in the capital in 2017 after a raid; men have been arrested for cross-dressing videos posted online. An international rights organisation reported in 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned after unfair trials over social media posts — including posts published before they entered the country — and device inspection at the border is an established risk.

The national tourism authority's "everyone is welcome" messaging reflects official interest in visitors' money, not any change in law. Any practical safety depends entirely on never being discovered, including digitally; detention would be in facilities matching passport sex, with no consular leverage able to prevent mistreatment.
blindOutOfScope: Missile and drone attacks on infrastructure, and the general risk of detention without charge for any visitor, affect all travellers.
blindSourceSummaries: Legal-services platform overview (June 2026): this country criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity - flogging, lengthy imprisonment and in the most severe cases death; no codified penal code (judges apply their own interpretation of religious law under the state's constitutional framework); no protections, no relationship recognition, no gender-transition pathway; explains how the system works without a penal code and what visitors need to know.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): penalties based on religious law with a maximum punishment of death; people suspected of homosexuality and trans women have been arrested, detained, tortured and prosecuted on morality grounds ('cross-dressing', 'offenses against religion', 'attacks against public morals'); known executions for same-sex intimacy usually involve additional charges; in 2019 the state security agency published a video categorising feminism and homosexuality as 'extremist ideas' punishable by prison and flogging.

Rights-group country review: deviation from traditional gender norms is a criminal offence under religious law (social behaviour, medical interventions, surgical transition); no explicit legislation but arrests and severe punishments including corporal retribution are common; gender-affirming healthcare permitted only for intersex people; the official religious-authority body rejects gender-affirming care and suggests prayer for gender dysphoria.

Encyclopedia overview: same-sex activity illegal with capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging, fines and deportation; no gender-identity recognition; sections on enforcement cases, censorship, living conditions, and HIV/AIDS (including treatment of foreigners).

A foreign broadcaster (May 2017): the transgender tailor who died in custody - arrested at a party of transgender foreign workers in the capital, imprisoned, and dead that night; activists from the workers' home country said he was beaten with clubs and hosepipes; the authorities said he had a heart attack.

Regional daily (Oct 2021): five men arrested for cross-dressing - they filmed themselves walking the streets in public and posted the video on social media; police said the conduct was 'inconsistent with the public morals of society'; criminal sanctions for cross-dressing mirror those for homosexuality (imprisonment, fines, deportation for foreigners).

International rights organisation with a regional human-rights monitoring group (June 2026, updated July 2026): visitors to this country - including tourists and religious pilgrims - risk detention, grossly unfair trials and lengthy prison sentences for their social media activity, including posts published before entering the country; eight documented cases (July 2022 to late 2025), predominantly involving visitors from poorer countries and other parts of the region.
A cable-news travel piece: this country's tourism authorities say LGBTQ visitors are 'welcome' even as same-sex conduct remains criminalised and travellers are urged to keep a low profile.

A foreign government's travel advice for this country: advises against all travel to parts and all but essential travel to other parts; safety and security, regional risks, pilgrimage guidance. General travel advice.

LGBTQ+ traveller risk map 2025 by a specialist monitoring firm, produced with travel-industry partners: country dossiers assessing traveller risk on 80+ criteria; a world map of safety for LGBTQ+ travellers with risk levels from 1 (lowest) upward, plus surveys and interviews with travel experts and community travellers.

Foreign broadsheet report (April 2005): dozens of men caught dancing and 'behaving like women' at a port-city party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced to a total of 14,200 lashes plus up to two years' jail, after a closed trial without defence lawyers; an international human-rights researcher called prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct flagrant human-rights violations.
blindTangential: Same-sex conduct punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment — a catastrophic formal exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
